name: Battle of Boyacá
info: A combined Venezuelan and New Granadan army with a British Legion under Simón Bolívar defeated Colonel José María Barreiro's Spanish III Division at Boyacá in 1819, opening the road to Santa Fe and the founding of Gran Colombia.

facts.date: 7 August 1819; the fighting lasted a little more than two hours and ended shortly after 4:30 p.m.
facts.place: Casa de Teja, beside the bridge over the Teatinos River on the Camino Real, about 150 km from Bogotá in the Andes, now in the Boyacá Department of Colombia
facts.sides: A Patriot army of Venezuelans, New Granadans and a British Legion under Simón Bolívar, with Brigadier Generals Francisco de Paula Santander and José Antonio Anzoátegui; the Spanish III Division of the Expeditionary Army of Costa Firme under Colonel José María Barreiro
facts.outcome: The Spanish division was effectively dismantled: 100 dead, 150 wounded and 1,600 captured, against 66 Patriot casualties. Viceroy Juan de Sámano fled Santa Fe two days later.

t: Bolívar's army crossed the Andes by the Páramo de Pisba in early July 1819, won narrowly at Vargas Swamp on 25 July, and then used a feint and a night countermarch to reach Tunja ahead of the Spanish.

On the day the Spanish vanguard and rearguard were split by the Patriot advance along the Camino Real and fought separately; the Patriots lost 13 dead and 53 wounded, the Spanish 100 dead, 150 wounded and 1,600 captured.
Within days the viceroy had fled Santa Fe, and in December 1819 New Granada and Venezuela were joined as the Republic of Colombia (Gran Colombia); 7 August is now a national holiday in Colombia.
dyk: The Spanish had carried their three artillery pieces unassembled, so when Arthur Sandes's Rifles charged the guns only one could be put together, and it fired three shots before its carriage broke.
ev: Bolívar's army crosses the Andes by the Páramo de Pisba and surprises the Spanish in the Boyacá region
Bolívar wins a narrow victory over Barreiro at the Battle of Vargas Swamp
A feint at the Chicamocha River and a night countermarch let Bolívar occupy Tunja and cut Barreiro's line to the capital
Barreiro marches round Tunja by Combita and Motavita towards Santa Fe
The Patriot vanguard and rearguard catch the Spanish at Casa de Teja and the Boyacá Bridge, and the Spanish division collapses in about two hours
Viceroy Sámano flees Santa Fe, and Bolívar enters the city on the 10th
Barreiro and 38 others are executed in Bogotá on Santander's orders

sections.background:
Simón Bolívar's Patriot Army surprised the Spanish by crossing the Andes through the Páramo de Pisba into the Boyacá region in early July 1819, though the march had weakened his army. Viceroy Juan de Sámano ordered Colonel José María Barreiro, an artillery officer who commanded the III Division of the Expeditionary Army of Costa Firme, the Spanish force in New Granada, to intercept and defeat Bolívar before he reached the capital, Santa Fe. The two forces met at the Battle of Vargas Swamp on 25 July, which Bolívar won narrowly.

Afterwards the Patriots camped near the battlefield and the Spanish at the town of Paipa. Both armies aimed at Santa Fe, which was defended by only some 400 Spanish troops. On 3 August the Spanish saw Bolívar's forces cross the Chicamocha River near Paipa, and at night saw him retreat to his earlier positions across it. They rested, unaware that this was a feint: Bolívar ordered a night countermarch, crossed the river again and took the alternative route to Tunja by the Toca road.

This put Bolívar ahead in the race to Santa Fe, reversing the earlier position. On 4 August he reached the village of Chivata at 9:00 a.m. and two hours later occupied Tunja, where he obtained 600 rifles. The city was lightly held, because its governor, Juan Lono, had left towards Paipa to bring Barreiro the supplies and reinforcements he had begged the viceroy for.
sections.forces:
The Patriot army was a combined force of Venezuelans and New Granadans together with a British Legion of British and Irish volunteers, under the overall command of Bolívar. Brigadier General Francisco de Paula Santander led its Vanguard Division and Brigadier General José Antonio Anzoátegui its Rearguard Division. Units named on the day include the Cazadores Battalion under Lieutenant Colonel Joaquín París, the battalions Barcelona and Bravos de Páez, the British Legion, the Rifles Battalion under Arthur Sandes.

The Spanish III Division under Barreiro included the 2nd and 3rd Numancia infantry battalions with some dragoons in its vanguard under Colonel Francisco Jiménez, and the King's 1st and 2nd infantry battalions, the Mounted Grenadiers and Dragoon cavalry. On 5 August Lono gave Barreiro 12,000 cartridges and three artillery pieces, two howitzers and one cannon. Barreiro, finding his line to the capital cut, marched round Tunja by night through mountain roads thought impassable in the rainy season. He left Combita at 1:00 a.m. on 6 August and reached Motavita at 11:30 a.m..

The Spanish left Motavita at 3:30 a.m. on 7 August to rejoin the Camino Real at Casa de Teja, where the Samacá road met it before it crossed the Boyacá Bridge over the Teatinos River, swollen by the rains. They covered the 25 km in 7 hours 30 minutes. From the San Lázaro heights near Tunja, Bolívar saw them at about 9:00 a.m. and worked out their route. A little after 10:00 he ordered Santander and Anzoátegui to set out along the Camino Real and destroy Barreiro wherever they found him.
sections.course:
Santander's vanguard left Tunja for Casa de Teja, about 16 km away, with Anzoátegui following, and the Patriots covered the distance in around four hours. Between noon and 1:00 p.m. the Spanish vanguard under Jiménez took position near Casa de Teja, stopped to eat. Shortly before 2:00 p.m. Captain Andrés Ibarra's Patriot party and the Spanish exchanged fire, and about 20 royalists chased it before returning on seeing a larger force. Santander ordered Lieutenant Colonel París to attack the Spanish at Casa de Teja.

The Spanish vanguard fell back across the Teatinos by the bridge. Santander sent Colonel Antonio Bejar down the river to cross it and take that vanguard from behind, while Anzoátegui moved to block the way between it and the Spanish rearguard, still several kilometres back. Outnumbered, the rearguard withdrew to a small hill near Casa de Teja, and Anzoátegui ordered a flank attack by Barcelona and Bravos de Páez on the right and the British Legion and the Rifles on the left.

Sandes's charge on the Spanish guns upset their assembly, and only one fired, three shots, before it broke. Bolívar sent lancers against the centre, and the Granadan Dragoons' charge was turned back by Patriot cavalry with longer lances. The Mounted Grenadiers left by the Samacá road, panic spread, and a bayonet charge ordered by the Spanish was not made. Barreiro and his officers dismounted trying to hold the rout and were captured. Bejar meanwhile forded the river, and Santander led a bayonet charge across the bridge. The Spanish fled, leaving Colonel Juan Tolrá dead on it.
sections.aftermath:
The fighting ended shortly after 4:30 p.m., having lasted a little more than two hours. The Patriots lost 66 men, some 13 dead and 53 wounded. Barreiro's III Division suffered 100 dead, 150 wounded and 1,600 captured, and was effectively dismantled. Barreiro himself and several other Spanish commanders were among the prisoners. Most of the prisoners were Venezuelans and New Granadans and were at once taken into the Patriot army, which grew considerably and could send units to parts of New Granada not yet liberated. Santander and Anzoátegui were promoted to General of Division.

A messenger rode 30 hours over the 100 km of bad road to Santa Fe, and the viceroy learned of the defeat at about 10:00 p.m. on 8 August. He left the capital at 9:00 a.m. on 9 August for Cartagena by way of Honda disguised as a peasant, leaving archives undestroyed and about 900,000 pesos in gold, silver and currency. That morning Colonel Sebastián de La Calzada blew up the arsenal's powder and left with the 400 troops in the city for Popayán, and royalist sympathisers and officials also fled.

Bolívar reached Santa Fe on 10 August with a cavalry group ahead of his army and was welcomed by the inhabitants. On 18 September a victory ceremony was held in the Plaza Mayor, where twenty women of prominent families dressed in white crowned him with a laurel wreath, and Bolívar, Santander and Anzoátegui received the Cruz de Boyacá, a medal made for the occasion. On 11 October Santander ordered Barreiro and 38 others executed in Bogotá, under the Decree of War to the Death.
sections.sources:
The battle is known through a detailed chronology of the march and the fighting, with the hours of departure, sighting and engagement set down, and with named units and officers on each side. The casualty figures stand as one set: 13 dead and 53 wounded for the Patriots, 100 dead, 150 wounded and 1,600 captured for the Spanish. The place of the fighting, Casa de Teja beside the Boyacá Bridge on the Teatinos, is identifiable, and the site is now dotted with monuments and statues. The bridge is no longer in use but is kept as a symbol of the independence of South America.

Details of who did what are not fully settled. Colonel Jiménez is named among the captured and Colonel Tolrá as killed on the bridge.
sections.legacy:
The battle is considered a crucial point in the independence of the north of South America. It ensured the success of Bolívar's campaign to liberate New Granada and allowed further Patriot victories at Carabobo in Venezuela, Pichincha in Ecuador, and Junín and Ayacucho in Peru. The defeat of the royal forces in central New Granada weakened the rest of the royal forces in America and ended Spanish control of the provinces there when the viceroy escaped. In December 1819 New Granada and Venezuela were united in the Republic of Colombia, called Gran Colombia. Fighting with royalist forces went on for years, and Venezuela, Peru and Ecuador became independent, and Bolivia was created, after a liberation campaign.

In Colombia 7 August is a national holiday. Every four years on that date the elected president takes the oath of office and receives the presidential sash in the Plaza de Bolívar in Bogotá. It is also Army Day, established officially in 1978 under President Alfonso López Michelsen, and on it the Colombian Army holds a large military ceremony at the site of the battle to commemorate the anniversary.

summary: At Boyacá on 7 August 1819 a Patriot army under Simón Bolívar caught the Spanish III Division under Barreiro as it marched for Santa Fe and in about two hours took 1,600 prisoners, for 66 casualties. The viceroy fled, and Gran Colombia followed in December.
notes: The article gives no strengths for either army; none are given in the text.

The lead says Barreiro and Colonel Francisco Jiménez were both captured; the battle section says only Barreiro's officers were taken and Colonel Juan Tolrá was killed on the bridge, and never says what became of Jiménez. The sources section says so.

The article's account of the Spanish vanguard and rearguard is confusing (the rearguard retreats to a hill, 'unable to cross the river' it takes position, and the 'Spanish rearguard' is later said to retreat); I followed the order given and left out the unclear direction.

The 'Consequences' list says the battle brought the end of Spanish control in 'the American provinces' and 'weakening of the rest of the forces in all America'; I wrote it with the article's own hedging as regards central New Granada.
Article has no contemporary sources or historiography; the sources section is therefore short and built on what the article has (casualty set, site, bridge, the Jiménez inconsistency).

The article spells the commander's name Barreiro, the hill and road names as given; accents added to Páez, Combita kept without accent as in article, Popayán, Sámano (article uses both Samano and Sámano).
